sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hrungnir** (*hrungnir*) ​— Giant, ‌Duel with Thor ‌· Brawler ​— is the ​strongest of ​the jötnar ​and the loser ​of the ‌most fully narrated ​single combat ​in Old Norse ‌myth: the ​stone-hearted giant who ‌wagered his ​head on his ‌stallion Gullfaxi ​against [[sleipnir|Sleipnir]], ​drank himself boastful ​in the ​hall of the ​gods, and ‌fell to Mjǫllnir ​at Grjótúnagarðar ‌with a whetstone ​in his ‌hand.[^1]

His story ​survives in ‌one sustained ​telling — Snorri's ‌Skáldskaparmál — ​resting on a ​verse witness ‌three centuries older: ‌the shield-poem ‌*Haustlöng* by Þjóðólfr ​of Hvin, ​composed in the ‌early tenth ​century and ​quoted by Snorri ‌as his ​authority.[^2] The myth's ​afterlife is ‌written into the ​world it ‌describes: the whetstone ​shattered against ​the hammer fathers ​every hone-rock ​on earth, ‌one shard stays ‌lodged in ​Thor's skull, and ‌the taboo ​against throwing whetstones ​across the ‌floor survived in ‌Scandinavian folk ‌custom as the ‌story's trace ​in daily ‌practice.[^1]

PuniCodex restores ​the name ​as **Hrungnir** — ​identical to ‌the ASCII input, ​because normalized ​Old Norse writes ​no diacritic ‌and no distinctive ​letter in ​this name; ​the mechanical rule ‌therefore places ​it in Tier ‌2, a ​statement about orthography ‌and never ​about the giant. ‌No domain ‌is claimed: the ​plain-ASCII *hrungnir.com* ​is registered ​to a third ​party outside ‌the collection and ‌is watched ​for release.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17–19 (the wager, the boasting in Valhǫll, the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Magni and Gróa), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Þjóðólfr ór Hvini, Haustlöng, stanzas quoted in Skáldskaparmál 17–19, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Hrungnir, Gullfaxi, Grjótúnagarðar.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Old Norse ‌as **Hrungnir** ​(nominative; genitive *Hrungnis*). ​Its etymology ​is one of ​the honest ​open questions of ‌the corpus: ​de Vries registers ​it without a ‌secure derivation, ​and the modern ‌handbooks — ​Simek, Orchard — ‌repeat the ​verdict that the ​name is ​unexplained.[^1] The PuniCodex ​lexicon's gloss, ​‘Brawler’, is a ‌project rendering ​of the figure's ‌role, not ​a claimed etymology; ‌the philological ​record offers nothing ‌firmer. The ​final *-r* is ‌the Old ​Norse masculine nominative ​ending, carried ‌in the ASCII ‌form itself.

Because ‌normalized Old ​Norse writes the ​name in ‌seven plain Latin ​letters, the ​Unicode restoration **Hrungnir** ‌is identical ​to the ASCII ​input apart ‌from the capital. ​There is ‌no diacritic and ​no distinctive ​letter to recover, ​and the ​mechanical tier rule ‌therefore classifies ‌the name Tier ​2: nothing ‌distinctive is lost ​in transit. The ​classification is ‌an orthographic report, ‌not a ‌judgment on the ‌myth.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation runs:

‌- **h** ​→ **H** — ​Same, capitalized
​- **r** → ‌**r** — ​Same
- **u** ​→ **u** ​— Same
- ‌**n** → ​**n** — Same
​- **g** ​→ **g** — ‌Same
- ​**n** → **n** ‌— Same
​- **i** → ‌**i** — Same
​- **r** ‌→ **r** — ‌Same

The ​project holds no ​domain for ​this name: *hrungnir.com* ​is held ‌outside the collection ‌and watched ​for release.[^2]

sources.citation: de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Hrungnir; Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hrungnir.
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Hrungnir.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name is ‌**/ˈhruŋɡ.nir/** — ​Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Hru-** ​— Aspirate ​[h] running straight ‌into trilled ​[r], then short ​close back ‌[u]; the initial ​*hr-* cluster ‌is genuine Old ​Norse, preserved ‌in words like ​*hringr* ‘ring’ ​where English later ​silenced the ​h
- **-ng-** ​— Velar ‌nasal [ŋ] plus ​a fully sounded ‌stop [g], ​as in English ‌*finger*; Old ​Norse sounded both, ‌never the ​bare nasal of ‌*singer*
- ​**-nir** — Second ​[n], short ‌[i], and the ‌final nominative ‌*-r*, lightly trilled

​For the ​modern speaker, the ‌closest approximation ​is: ‘HRUNG-nir’ — ​breathy h, ‌a short ‘oo’ ​as in ​*put*, both the ‌ng and ​the g sounded, ‌and a ​trill at the ​end.

Kindred ​and historical forms ​of the ‌name:

- **Old ‌Norse** — ​Hrungnir, strongest of ‌the jötnar; ​no agreed etymology
​- **Younger ‌Futhark** — ᚼᚱᚢᚴᚾᛁᛦ, ‌the Viking-Age ‌runic rendering (h-r-u-k-n-i-R); ‌ᚴ writes ​both k and ‌g, and ​ᛦ carries the ​final nominative ​-r[^2]
- **Skaldic ‌attestation** — Hrungnir, ​named in ​Þjóðólfr of Hvin's ​*Haustlöng* (early ‌10th c.), the ​name's oldest ​sustained witness

The ​stress falls ‌on the first ​syllable, as ‌in every Old ​Norse word. ‌Hrungnir is Tier ​2 because ‌the restoration preserves ‌nothing the ​ASCII alphabet loses: ​the name ​was plain ASCII ​all along, ‌in the manuscripts ‌as on ​the keyboard.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Barnes, Michael P., Runes: A Handbook (Woodbridge: Boydell Press, 2012), on the younger futhark's underspecification of stop voicing.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌medieval Icelandic ​manuscripts ​in the ​Latin alphabet ​as **Hrungnir** ​— ‌Old Norse ​(North Germanic), ​attested ‌13th–14th c. ​CE in ‌the Codex ​Regius ‌of the ​Prose Edda ​and related ​codices, ​quoting verse ​composed in ‌the early ​tenth ‌century.[^1] No ​runic attestation ‌survives, so ​the ‌manuscript form ​is the ‌primary witness; ​a ​younger-futhark rendering ‌would run ‌ᚼᚱᚢᚴᚾᛁᛦ ‌(h-r-u-k-n-i-R).

The ​scholarly rendering ​proceeds step ‌by ​step:

- ​The name ‌is a ​single ​opaque element ‌plus the ​masculine nominative ‌ending ​*-r*; its ​etymology is ​unresolved in ​the ‌standard handbooks.
‌- The ​initial cluster ‌*hr-* ​and the ​medial *-ng-* ‌are ‌sounded in ‌full: /ˈhruŋɡ.nir/, ‌with the ​stop ‌g pronounced ​after the ​velar nasal.
​- ‌Normalized Old ​Norse orthography ​writes no ​diacritic ‌in this ​name; the ​Unicode restoration ​**Hrungnir** ‌is therefore ​identical to ‌the ASCII ​input ‌apart from ​the capital, ‌and ‌the tier ​rule classifies ​it Tier ​2 ​— an ‌orthographic fact, ‌not a ​judgment.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Hrungnir.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Hrungnir** is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ‌‘Giant, Duel ​with Thor’ ​— and ​the sources ​earn both ​halves of it.[^1]

‌### The ​Giant

Snorri's ​formula is ‌that Hrungnir ​was the ‌strongest of ​all the ‌jötnar, with a ​heart of ​stone — ​three-cornered and ​sharp-edged — ​a head ‌of stone, ​and a ‌broad shield of ​stone: a ‌giant made ​of his ‌own weapon's ​material, the ‌mountainside given ​intent.

### ​The Duel

The ‌challenge at ‌Grjótúnagarðar is ‌the corpus's ​most complete ​single combat: ‌appointed ground, ​seconds, terms, ​and a throw-for-throw ‌exchange of ​missiles — ​the whetstone ‌against the ​hammer — ‌narrated like ​a formal ​hólmganga between worlds.

​### The ​Wager

Before ‌the duel ‌comes the ​race: [[odinn|Óðinn]] ‌wagers his ​head that ​no horse in ‌[[jotunheimr|Jötunheimr]] matches ‌Sleipnir, and ‌Hrungnir's fury ‌at the ​boast carries ‌him past ​his own ​frontier and into ​the hall ‌of the ​gods.

### ​The Aftermath

​The myth ‌keeps its ​strangest weight ​for after the ​killing: Hrungnir ‌falls forward ​across [[thor|Þórr]], ‌his foot ​on the ‌god's neck, ​and all ‌the Æsir together ‌cannot lift ​it — ​until three-night-old ​[[magni|Magni]] throws ​it off ‌and earns ‌Gullfaxi for ​the deed.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17–19, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography of ‌Hrungnir is ‌the iconography ​of stone: ​the corpus ​dresses him ​in his ​own geology.[^1]

‌- ​**The whetstone** ​— his ‌hone, hurled ​with both ‌hands against ​Mjǫllnir: the ‌stone whose ​purpose is ​sharpening ​other things, ​shattered on ​the first ‌iron it ​met; its ‌fallen half ​fathers every ‌hone-rock ​in the ‌world, its ​flying half ‌still sits ​in Thor's ​head
- ‌**Gullfaxi** — ‌‘golden mane’, ‌the ​stallion whose ​speed was ‌worth a ​giant's head ​in Óðinn's ‌wager, and ​which ends ​the story ‌in ​the hands ‌of a ​three-night-old god
​- **The ​three-cornered stone ​heart** — ‌courage of ‌the wrong ​material: ‌hard, sharp-edged, ​and entirely ​without flexibility
‌- **Mǫkkurkálfi** ‌— ‘mist-calf’, ‌the giants' ‌clay champion, ​nine leagues ‌tall ​and three ​across the ​chest, given ‌a mare's ​heart for ​want of ​a bigger ‌one: ​the archetype ​of size ​without courage[^2]
‌- **The ​fallen foot** ‌— the ​leg across ‌Thor's neck ​that ‌all the ‌Æsir together ​could not ​shift: the ​weight of ​the foe ‌after the ‌foe is ​dead

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17–19, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hrungnir, Mokkurkalfi.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Hrungnir's mythology is a ​single arc — wager, boast, duel, aftermath ‌— told once at length in Skáldskaparmál ‌and vouched for by the oldest mythological ​praise-poem we have.[^1]

### The Wager of ​Heads (Skáldskaparmál 17)

Riding [[sleipnir|Sleipnir]] through Jötunheimr, ​[[odinn|Óðinn]] meets Hrungnir, who asks who the ​gold-helmed rider is and praises the horse. ​Óðinn wagers his head that no horse ‌in Jötunheimr is Sleipnir's equal; Hrungnir springs ​to Gullfaxi and gives chase in a ​fury — and, carried past his own ‌turning, gallops through the gates of [[asgardr|Ásgarðr]] ​itself.

### Drunk in the Hall of ‌the Gods (Skáldskaparmál 17)

The Æsir set ​before him the horns Thor drank from, ‌and Hrungnir empties them all. Drunk, he ​lets the boasts out: he will carry ​[[valholl|Valhǫll]] off to Jötunheimr, sink Ásgarðr, kill ​every god save [[freyja|Freyja]] and [[sif|Sif]], whom ​he will carry home — and drink ​all the mead himself. The Æsir name ‌Thor; Thor comes in swinging his hammer ​and demands who gave jötnar leave to ‌drink in Valhǫll. Hrungnir, under Óðinn's safe-conduct, ​claims the rights of an unarmed man: ‌Thor will win little honour killing him ​as he is. Let him dare single ‌combat instead, at the frontier, at Grjótúnagarðar. ​Thor, Snorri says, would by no means ‌refuse.[^1]

### The Whetstone and the Hammer ​(Skáldskaparmál 17–19)

The giants make much of ​the appointment — Hrungnir is their strongest, ‌and they expect the outcome to decide ‌everything — and they build him a ‌second of clay: Mǫkkurkálfi, nine leagues tall, ​with a mare's heart quaking inside. Hrungnir ​stands with his stone heart, stone head, ‌and stone shield, holding his hone. Þjálfi ​runs ahead and calls that Thor is ​coming from below; Hrungnir sets the shield ‌beneath his feet and stands on it. ​Thor comes in lightning and hurls Mjǫllnir ​from afar; Hrungnir throws the hone with ‌both hands, and the weapons meet in ​the air. The hone bursts: one half ‌falls to earth — from it come ​all the whetstone rocks — and one ​half drives into Thor's head. But the ​hammer does not stop: it crushes Hrungnir's ​skull, and the giant falls forward across ‌Thor, his foot on the god's neck. ‌Þjálfi goes at Mǫkkurkálfi, and the clay ​giant falls with little glory.[^1]

### The ‌Foot and the Forgotten Spell (Skáldskaparmál 19)

​Neither Thor nor Þjálfi can shift the ​foot; all the Æsir come and cannot ‌lift it. At last comes [[magni|Magni]], Thor's ‌son by Járnsaxa, three nights old, and ‌throws it off, saying he thinks he ‌would have struck the giant dead with ​his fist; Thor gives him Gullfaxi, and ‌Óðinn objects that the fine horse has ​gone to a giantess's son rather than ​his own father. The hone stays in ​Thor's head. The völva Gróa, wife of ‌Aurvandill the Bold, comes to sing it ​loose, and the stone is already working ​free — until Thor, to please her, ​tells how he carried Aurvandill out of ‌Jötunheimr in a basket and set his ​frozen toe in the sky as a ​star. Gróa rejoices so greatly that she ​forgets her spells, and the hone stirs ‌in Thor's head to this day; therefore, ​Snorri warns, whetstones must never be thrown ‌across the floor.[^1]

### The Skaldic Witness ​(Haustlöng)

Snorri's authority is Þjóðólfr of Hvin's ‌*Haustlöng*, a shield-poem of the early tenth ​century: the combat, the shaking earth, the ‌whetstone, and the fall are all there ‌in dense dróttkvætt, proving the story was ​already old and fixed three centuries before ​Snorri wrote it down.[^2] Within the corpus, ​Hrungnir's duel stands between Thor's other named ​giant-fights — [[geirrodr|Geirröðr]], killed by a thrown ‌glowing iron, and the fishing for the ‌World Serpent — as the hardest fight ​the thunderer ever won.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17–19, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Þjóðólfr ór Hvini, Haustlöng, stanzas quoted in Skáldskaparmál 17–19, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hrungnir, Thor.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Hrungnir ​resists the ‌usual syncretic ‌moves. The ​temptation to ​read him ​as a ​reflex of ​the ‌Indo-European chaos-combat ​— a ​stone-bodied being ‌struck down ​by the ‌thunderer's missile, ​on the ‌pattern ​of Vedic ​Vṛtra — ​has been ​tried, but ​the fit ‌is partial: ​Hrungnir steals ‌nothing, ​hoards nothing, ‌and holds ​back no ‌waters. The ​handbooks treat ‌the duel ​as a ​native ‌Norse contest-epic ‌rather than ‌an inherited ​dragon-slaying.[^1]

His ​truer company ‌is within ​the corpus ​itself. ‌He is ​one of ​the named ‌great fights ​of Þórr, ‌standing beside ​[[geirrodr|Geirröðr]] — ​killed ​by a ​glowing iron ‌thrown back ‌at its ​sender — ‌and the ​near-fatal fishing ​expedition ‌against the ‌Miðgarðsormr; each ‌fight tests ‌the same ​question with ‌a different ​weapon. The ​shard ​lodged in ‌Thor's skull ​has been ​compared with ​the embedded, ‌unremovable weapons ​of other ​traditions, ​but no ‌source demonstrates ​a borrowing, ‌and scholarship ​registers Hrungnir ‌as a ​distinctively northern ‌invention: ‌a giant ​built of ​the very ​landscape the ​North knew ‌— stone, ‌clay, and ​weather.[^2]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hrungnir, Thor.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hrungnir.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Hrungnir's ​afterlife runs ‌through the ‌skalds before ​it runs ​through anyone ​else. *Haustlöng* ​made his ​fall ‌one of ​the foundation-texts ​of Old ‌Norse poetics ​— Snorri ‌quotes it ​as the ‌authority ​for the ​myth — ​so every ​student of ​skaldic verse ‌meets the ​stone-hearted giant ‌early, ​embedded in ‌the densest ​metre the ‌tradition produced.[^1]

​The myth's ‌debris entered ​folklore. The ​aetiology ‌of the ‌hone-rocks and ‌the taboo ​against throwing ​whetstones across ‌the floor ​— lest ​the ‌shard stir ​in Thor's ​head — ‌survived in ​Scandinavian folk ‌collections as ​a curiosity ​of ​thunder-lore long ​after the ‌god had ‌faded.[^2] In ​modern reception, ‌Hrungnir is ​the template ​for ‌every stone-hearted ‌colossus the ‌fantasy genre ‌has built ​since: games ‌and novels ​reach for ​his ​duel whenever ‌a hero ​must fight ​a mountain ​that can ‌throw back. ​His name ​never ​entered living ‌use the ​way Baldr's ‌or Thor's ​did; it ‌remains exactly ​what the ‌Edda ‌made it ​— the ​name of ​the strongest ​thing the ‌hammer ever ‌had to ​kill.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Haustlöng, Hrungnir.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hrungnir.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​cult site, ‌votive deposit, ‌runestone, or ​securely ​identified image ​of Hrungnir ​is known; ​his attestation ‌is ​literary.[^1] The ​material witness ‌is instead ​a ‌poem about ​an object: ‌*Haustlöng* was ​composed for ​a ​painted shield ​— a ​Viking-Age prestige ‌object ​bearing mythic ‌scenes — ​and the ‌stanzas ​Snorri preserves ‌are our ​evidence that ‌the Hrungnir ​combat ​belonged to ‌that visual ‌repertoire in ‌the ​early tenth ​century, within ‌the lifetime ​of the ​pagan ‌courts.

The ​myth's own ​materiality is ‌geological: ​Snorri anchors ‌the shattered ​whetstone in ​the ​landscape itself, ​deriving every ‌hone-rock from ‌its fallen ​half, ‌and the ​household taboo ​on thrown ‌whetstones ‌carried the ‌story into ‌daily practice.[^2] ​The literary ‌witnesses ​hang by ​the usual ​threads: Skáldskaparmál ‌in ​the Codex ​Regius of ​the Prose ‌Edda ​and its ​sister manuscripts, ​and the ‌*Haustlöng* stanzas ​surviving ‌nowhere but ​in Snorri's ‌quotation — ​a ‌giant preserved ‌twice over, ​in prose ​and in ​the ​verse the ‌prose was ‌written to ​explain.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hrungnir, Haustlöng.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 19 (the hone in Thor's head and the whetstone taboo), trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The ​Poetic Edda ‌proper ‌is silent ​on Hrungnir: ​no ​poem of ​the ​Codex Regius ‌names him, ​stages ​the wager, ‌or ​remembers Grjótúnagarðar.[^1] ‌The corpus's ​verse ‌witness is ​skaldic ​instead — ​Þjóðólfr of ​Hvin's ​*Haustlöng*, composed ‌in ​the early ‌tenth ​century for ‌a painted ​shield ‌and preserved ​only ‌because Snorri ​quoted it, ​stanza ‌by stanza, ‌to ‌document the ​myth.

That ​distribution ‌is itself ​instructive. ​Hrungnir belongs ‌to the ​world ​of the ‌praise-poem ​and the ‌prose ​treatise rather ​than the ​mythological ​lay: his ‌combat ‌was court ​poetry's property, ‌a ​scene a ​patron's ‌shield could ‌carry, three ‌centuries ‌before Snorri ​made ‌it prose. ​Where the ​Eddic ​poems stage ‌Thor's ​contests as ​dialogue ​and insult ‌— Þrymskviða's ​bridal ​farce, Hárbarðsljóð's ​flyting ‌— the ​Hrungnir duel ‌comes ​down to ‌us ​as spectacle, ‌narrated in ‌dróttkvætt ​kennings dense ​enough ​that Snorri's ​prose retelling ‌is ‌nearly a ​commentary.[^2]

sources.citation: The Poetic Edda, trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014) — the corpus contains no attestation of Hrungnir.
Þjóðólfr ór Hvini, Haustlöng, stanzas quoted in Skáldskaparmál 17–19, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The ​Prose Edda ‌is Hrungnir's ‌sole narrative ​home, and ​Skáldskaparmál ​17–19 gives ​him the ​fullest giant-combat ‌in ​the corpus: ​the wager ‌of heads ​over Sleipnir's ‌speed, ​the drunken ‌boasting in ​Valhǫll under ​Óðinn's safe-conduct, ​the ​challenge claimed ​as an ‌unarmed guest's ​right, ‌the appointed ​ground at ‌Grjótúnagarðar, the ​clay second ‌with ​the mare's ‌heart, Þjálfi's ​ruse that ​puts ‌the shield ‌under Hrungnir's ‌feet, the ​mid-air collision ​of ‌hone and ​hammer, and ​the double ‌aftermath — ​Magni's ​three-night-old feat ‌of strength ​and Gróa's ‌forgotten ​spell that ​leaves the ​whetstone in ​Thor's skull.[^1]

‌Snorri's ‌method deserves ​note: he ‌interrupts his ​own narrative ​to ‌quote Þjóðólfr's ‌*Haustlöng* as ‌documentary proof, ‌treating ​the tenth-century ‌shield-poem as ​the primary ​record and ​his ‌prose as ​its explanation ​— an ​unusually ‌transparent piece ​of medieval ​source-criticism.[^2] Elsewhere ​the Prose ‌Edda ​keeps Hrungnir ‌in its ​systematic apparatus: ‌the þulur ​count ‌him in ‌the name-lists ​of the ​jötnar, ​preserving in ​catalogue form ‌the giant ‌the narrative ​spends.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17–19, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Þjóðólfr ór Hvini, Haustlöng, quoted in Skáldskaparmál 17–19, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, þulur (name-lists of the jötnar), ed. and trans. Faulkes, Edda: Skáldskaparmál (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The ​runic corpus ‌contains ‌no attestation ​of ​Hrungnir: no ​runestone ​names ​him, no ‌amulet ​invokes him, ​and ‌the element ​*hrungn-* ‌appears in ​no ‌recorded anthroponym.[^1] ​The ​name's raw ​materials ​are nonetheless ​ordinary ‌runic ​stock — ‌the ​corpus preserves ‌the ​initial *hr-* ‌cluster ​and medial ‌*-ng-* ​in many ​personal ‌names, so ‌the ‌theonym is ​phonologically ​at ‌home in ​the ​runic period ‌even ​though the ​carving ‌itself never ​happened.

‌A Viking-Age ​rendering ​would run ​**ᚼᚱᚢᚴᚾᛁᛦ** ​(h-r-u-k-n-i-R) in ‌the ‌younger ​futhark, and ‌the ​usual underspecification ​applies: ‌the sixteen-rune ‌row ‌writes both ‌k ​and g ‌with ​ᚴ and ​the ​final nominative ‌-r ​with ​ᛦ, so ​the ‌carving would ​say ​less than ​the ‌manuscripts do.[^2] ​The ‌manuscript spelling ​of ‌the Prose ​Edda ‌remains the ‌primary ​witness ​— and ​it ​is, like ‌the ‌restoration, plain ​ASCII.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hrungnir.
Barnes, Michael P., Runes: A Handbook (Woodbridge: Boydell Press, 2012).

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond ​the Eddas, ‌Hrungnir's medieval ‌afterlife ​is thin ​and telling. ​The ​þulur — ​the metrical ‌name-lists ​appended to ​the ‌Prose Edda ​— keep ‌him ​catalogued among ‌the jötnar, ​a ​giant reduced ​from protagonist ​to ​entry; and ‌skaldic poets ​long ‌after Þjóðólfr ​could still ‌reach ​for the ‌combat ​in kennings ‌for shields, ​stones, ​and Thor's ‌hammer, where ‌the ‌audience was ​trusted to ​know ‌the whole ​story from ​a ‌shard of ​it.[^1]

The ​great ‌silence is ​Saxo's. ‌The *Gesta ​Danorum*, which ​retells ​so many ​of Thor's ‌fights ‌in euhemerized ​form, gives ‌no ​corresponding role ​to a ‌Hrungnir, ‌and Heimskringla's ‌prose mythology ‌passes ​him by ‌as ​well.[^2] The ​tradition's verdict ​is ‌consistent: Hrungnir ​had one ​story, ​it belonged ‌to one ​shield-poem ​and one ​prose treatise, ‌and ​no saga-writer ‌ever found ​a ‌second use ​for ‌him — ‌the strongest ​of ​the jötnar, ​spent entirely ​in ‌a single ‌afternoon at ​Grjótúnagarðar.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, þulur (jötunn name-lists), ed. and trans. Faulkes, Edda: Skáldskaparmál (Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979) — no counterpart to Hrungnir appears.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Hrungnir ​is the ‌Edda's essay ‌on confidence ​without ​flexibility. Every ​part of ​him ​is the ‌hardest available ​material — ​heart ‌of stone, ​head of ‌stone, ​shield of ‌stone — ​and the ​myth's ​arithmetic is ​that hardness ​is ‌not the ​same as ‌strength. The ​whetstone ‌is the ​perfect weapon ‌for ​him: a ‌stone whose ​entire purpose ​is ‌to sharpen ‌other things, ‌hurled ​once and ​shattered on ‌the first ​iron ​it meets.[^1]

‌Against him ​the ​story sets ‌two counter-images. ​Mǫkkurkálfi, the ‌engineered ​champion — ​nine leagues ​of ​clay around ‌a mare's ‌heart — ​is ‌the warning ​about size ​without ‌courage. And ‌Magni, three ‌nights old, ‌lifting ​what all ‌the Æsir ​together ​could not, ​is the ‌warning about ​measuring ​strength by ​age, rank, ‌or ​expectation. Hrungnir ​wagered his ​head on ‌a ​horse race ‌and lost ​it ‌in a ​duel; the ‌strongest thing ‌in ​the room ​is a ​wager ​too, and ‌someone always ‌holds the ​hammer.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál 17–19, trans. Faulkes (1987).
